extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in humor theory (students, researchers, comedy writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply Thomas C. Veatch's 'Affective Absurdity' theory of humor: conditions under which events become humorous and practical implications for crafting or analyzing jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous normality and violation (N and V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous situations arise when an event/situation is simultaneously perceived as normal (N) and as a violation (V) of some affective commitment of the perceiver to the way something in the situation should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veatch's core claim: both factors must be present; if one of these three factors is not present then humour will not arise. Use the N/V framing when analyzing why an instance is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence requirement (both factors necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of the factors (normality or violation) is missing then humour will not arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a joke, check that there is a recognizable 'normal' element and a perceived violation; absence of either suggests the material won't read as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative strength/balance of N and V
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived humour depends on the relative strengths of the V and N interpretations: if V is proportionally far greater than N, it's likely to be perceived as threatening or offensive; if V is much weaker than N, it may be interpreted as non-humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the balance: effective humor often requires V and N to be roughly comparable in strength. When crafting jokes, avoid letting V overwhelm N (risking offense) or letting N overwhelm V (yielding blandness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral attachment predicts responses (Predictions 1 & 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X finds a situation funny where a principle is violated and Y finds it offensive, frightening, or threatening, then Y is more attached to the violated principle than X. If someone finds it unremarkable, they have no personal moral attachment to the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perceived moral attachment to predict audience reaction: offended audiences likely have stronger commitments to the violated principle; indifferent audiences lack attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachment (others vs. self)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation that happens to others is not felt as strongly as one that happens to oneself; this shifts interpretation from threat/offense (V predominates) to humor (N predominates) when the object of the violation is another rather than oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling jokes about others (vs. oneself) or creating distance can increase likelihood of humor; consider target and perspective when predicting acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distance reduces emotional involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassing or painful events may not seem funny immediately but may become funny as time passes because the person is 'less emotionally involved in the particular instance of violating the principles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing time between violation and joke can shift audience response from offense to amusement; temporal framing is a tool for managing the V/N balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of elements (N+V vs V+N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes follow an order of N + V (normal situation revealed then violated), although humorous situations may arise in either order N+V or V+N. The order affects the type of effect produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with setup/punchline ordering: N+V is common, but V+N (set up an exotic/strange scene, then a mundane punchline) can also work. Match order to desired comic effect (surprise, relief, incongruity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief and disbelief patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief laughter occurs when something bad is presented (V) followed by something perceived as good (V+N). Likewise, sudden bad news may produce a moment of laughter through disbelief (N+V) before belief fastens and all humour is lost (V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the joke aims to produce relief (resolving V into N) or a brief disbelief laugh (initial N+V); structure timing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety of teller and performance can shift balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong V interpretation may be matched by a strongly motivated N interpretation, so that even something quite offensive or threatening can be made to seem funny if, for example, a joke is told well enough, or is told by someone felt to be 'safe'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider teller identity, tone, and delivery: skill and perceived 'safety' of performer can increase the N interpretation and make risky material land as humor rather than offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity magnification by increasing components
rubrics_metrics.description: The intensity of a joke may be magnified if any of the components that make it up are increased: more perceived violations, a principle violated that is extremely relevant, or a particularly gratifying sense of normality can all increase funniness, assuming relative balance remains acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To heighten impact, amplify V and/or N elements—but monitor balance so V does not become disproportionately large and turn into offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's psychological effects (normalization vs offense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can have both positive and negative psychological effects: by making a perceived violation 'normal' the attachment to the violated principle may be lessened, but laughing at a normal situation or perceived mockery of the normal may become offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of downstream effects: using humor to normalize behavior can change attitudes, but can also alienate audiences who feel their principles are being demeaned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting setup/punchline contrast (elaborate strange setup + mundane punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the elaboration of an unusual or exotic setup while keeping the punchline as mundane as possible gives the joke the best chance of succeeding; however, making the violation too extreme runs the risk of offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing jokes, make the setup sufficiently odd/complex and the punchline mundane to maximize N/V contrast, but check audience sensitivity to avoid tipping V too far.
